Patagonia is at the centre of this trip. The pace changes as you leave the cities behind and take to long roads through steppe and mountains, past glaciers, cold lakes and national parks. Beyond Patagonia, you’ll find marine wildlife on the Valdés Peninsula, forests and lakes around Bariloche, the dry highlands of Salta and the subtropical forests of Iguazú.

## How the trip unfolds

The first few days are in Chile. Santiago introduces you to the capital, while Valparaíso and Viña del Mar take you to the Pacific coast. From there, you head straight south into the wildest stretch of the trip.

Visiting Torres del Paine and El Calafate back to back makes Patagonia feel like one continuous leg. You’ll start with granite mountains, lakes and guanacos, then move on to ice fields and the Perito Moreno Glacier. Between them, you’ll cross the Chile–Argentina border on a road through the dry steppe.

From Ushuaia, you’ll explore Tierra del Fuego on two separate days, one on an off-road trip to the lakes and the other in the national park. The trip then reaches the Atlantic at the Valdés Peninsula, where two days are set aside for watching marine wildlife.

Around Bariloche, you’ll see a greener side of Patagonia. The route takes in Lake Nahuel Huapi, Victoria Island, the Arrayanes Forest, the Route of the Seven Lakes and the Small Circuit. This part of the trip has fewer long flights and more time on scenic roads, on a catamaran and at viewpoints.

From Bariloche, the itinerary heads north to Salta. The Hill of Seven Colours, Humahuaca, the salt flats and Los Cardones show you the dry highlands of northwestern Argentina. Iguazú follows, with three days around the tropical forest and waterfalls.

The trip ends in Buenos Aires. After three weeks outdoors, you can slow down, explore the main neighbourhoods, see a tango show and spend a day at a ranch. Optional visits to Tigre and Montevideo give you more ways to spend these last days.

## A closer look at the itinerary

In Ushuaia, there’s time to explore both the mountain and coastal sides of Tierra del Fuego. From Garibaldi Pass, you can look out over lakes Escondido and Fagnano. A four-wheel-drive vehicle takes you along old forest tracks, and the national park brings you to the Beagle Channel. In town, you can also visit the history museum and the old prison. The region is known for the End of the World Train and for ski routes through Garibaldi Pass, forests, peat bogs and lakes.

Two days on the Valdés Peninsula give you more time to look for marine wildlife, which varies with the season and conditions. You’ll spend the first day entirely on the peninsula. The second starts with another chance to see whales and other coastal wildlife before you fly to Bariloche.

You’ll spend four days getting to know Bariloche. After a long journey, your first evening introduces you to the town on Lake Nahuel Huapi. The next day, you’ll travel by catamaran to Victoria Island and the Arrayanes Forest. You’ll then follow the Route of the Seven Lakes. Before your flight to Salta, you’ll do the Small Circuit, stopping at Playa Bonita and going up Cerro Campanario. You’ll see the region from the water, from the road and from above.

You’ll spend three days in northwestern Argentina. Humahuaca introduces you to the region’s history and culture, with Indigenous fortifications, old settlements and colonial churches close together. The next day takes you to the salt flats along a mountain road. Los Cardones shows another side of the highlands, with towering old cacti and wide open spaces.

You’ll have time to see Iguazú from several angles. After arriving and checking in, you’ll visit the Brazilian side, with a walking trail, Macuco, the Bird Park and a helicopter flight. You’ll then spend a full day on the Argentine side. You’ll see the falls from panoramic viewpoints, from the water, from above and up close on the walkways.

Your last days in Buenos Aires combine a city tour with separate cultural outings. The tango show comes with dinner and a transfer. The ranch day includes empanadas, horse riding, an asado, folk entertainment and gaucho demonstrations. If you’d prefer to spend more time exploring cities and waterways, you can choose Tigre or Montevideo in place of the ranch.

## Transport and accommodation

The trip includes many flights and road transfers. These are spaced to leave time for the main excursions. In Chile, after Santiago, you’ll go straight to a hotel inside Torres del Paine, opposite Grey Glacier. The itinerary lists Arakur in Ushuaia, Territorio on the Valdés Peninsula and Villa Beluno in Bariloche. In Iguazú, you’ll stay at Belmond Iguazu, and in Buenos Aires you’ll stay at Four Seasons Buenos Aires with breakfast.

The longest drives are in Patagonia and northwestern Argentina. The transfer from Puerto Natales to El Calafate takes about 4–5 hours. The drives to Humahuaca and to the salt flats each take 2–3 hours one way on mountain roads. Domestic flights link these parts of the itinerary to leave more time for excursions.

Allow about 40 minutes to reach the airport in Santiago, about two hours from Puerto Natales to Torres del Paine, about 40 minutes from Ushuaia airport to Arakur, about an hour from Trelew to the Valdés Peninsula and about 40 minutes from Buenos Aires airport to Four Seasons. These transfers are part of the itinerary and give you a sense of the pace on travel days.
